title: Phrasal verbs and collocations
grammar: Separable and inseparable phrasal verbs, collocations

sections.heading: What is a phrasal verb?
sections.body: A phrasal verb is a verb + preposition/adverb that has a meaning different from the original verb. Example: 'give up' does not mean 'give' + 'up', it means 'stop doing something'.

sections.heading: Types of phrasal verbs
table: I ran into an old friend.
verb + object + particle OR verb + particle + object
Turn off the light. / Turn the light off.

sections.heading: Separable phrasal verbs
sections.body: With separable phrasal verbs, the object can go between the verb and the particle, or after the particle. But if the object is a pronoun, it MUST go between them.

sections.heading: High-frequency phrasal verbs
table: He came up with a great idea.
Please carry on with your work.
They set up a small company.
I can't deal with this problem.

sections.heading: Collocations
sections.body: A collocation is a combination of words that naturally go together. Learning collocations makes your English sound more natural.
table: We need to make a decision.
I have a shower every morning.
Please pay attention to the instructions.
You should not break the rules.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
list: Do not separate inseparable phrasal verbs: 'I ran an old friend into' is wrong.
Pronouns must go in the middle of separable phrasal verbs: 'Turn it off', not 'Turn off it'.
Do not translate phrasal verbs literally from Spanish.

phases.name: Discovery
phases.intro: Look at these sentences. Read them carefully and think about the questions below.
sentences: I ran into an old friend at the supermarket yesterday.
We have run out of milk. Can you buy some?
She came up with a great idea.
They put off the meeting until Friday.
I get along well with my colleagues.
questions: In sentences 1, 2, 6 and 8, which phrasal verbs are inseparable?
In sentences 3, 4 and 5, what is the difference between the three orders?
In sentence 5, why is 'it' in the middle?
In sentence 7, can we say 'They put the meeting off'? Why?

questions.prompt: I ___ an old teacher at the supermarket yesterday.
questions.explanation: Run into means to meet by chance.

questions.prompt: We have ___ milk. Can you buy some?
questions.explanation: Run out of means to have no more of something.

questions.prompt: Turn ___ the light, please. It's dark.
questions.explanation: Turn on means to switch on.

questions.prompt: She ___ a brilliant idea.
questions.explanation: Come up with = to think of an idea.

questions.prompt: They ___ the meeting until Friday.
I ___ well with my new colleagues.
questions.explanation: Get along with = have a good relationship.

questions.prompt: Don't ___ ! Keep trying.
Can you ___ me ___ at the station?
We need to ___ a decision today.
Please ___ attention to the instructions.

sections.heading: Key rules
list: Phrasal verbs = verb + particle, with a new meaning.
Three types: intransitive, transitive inseparable, transitive separable.
With separable phrasal verbs, pronouns must go in the middle: turn it off.
Inseparable: look after, run into, get along with, come up with, deal with.
Separable: turn on/off, pick up, put off, hand in.
Collocations: make a decision, take a risk, pay attention, keep in touch.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
list: Do not separate inseparable phrasal verbs.
Pronouns go in the middle of separable phrasal verbs.
Do not translate phrasal verbs literally from Spanish.

sections.heading: Useful phrases
list: Give up, find out, get along, put off, look after, run out of, come up with, carry on, set up, deal with.
Make a decision, take a risk, pay attention, keep in touch, break the news, make an effort.
